cards.headline: The numbers can whisper trouble.
cards.body: A collapse rarely arrives without warning. It shows up first as small contradictions in the statements — profit that never becomes cash, inventory piling up, "one-time" charges that arrive every year. Learning to read those tells is half of protecting your money.

cards.headline: Profit up, cash down.
cards.body: The loudest red flag: reported earnings climbing while operating cash flow falls. Real profit eventually turns into cash. When the two pull apart for long, the profit may be an accounting story — often revenue booked faster than customers actually pay.

art.name: cash-vs-profit
art.alt: A rising profit line diverging from a falling cash line, warning that earnings are not turning into cash.

cards.title: Receivables outrunning sales
cards.caption: When receivables or inventory sprint ahead of sales, customers may be paying slower — or the goods just aren't selling.

cards.prompt: Sales rose 12% but accounts receivable jumped 38%. Reassuring, or a closer look?
cards.explanation: Receivables outrunning sales means revenue is booked but not yet collected — from customers paying slower, or aggressive terms propping up the top line. Dig into why.

cards.headline: "One-time" every single year.
cards.body: A charge is only extraordinary if it happens once. When "non-recurring" costs recur annually, they are just costs in a costume. Watch, too, for buybacks funded with borrowed money and dividends larger than free cash flow — returns paid from the balance sheet, not the business.
Some warnings sit outside the ratios — in who keeps the books and how insiders behave.
When a company's "one-time" charges appear year after year, they are not exceptional — they are recurring [[1]] in disguise.
cards.explanation: A genuinely one-off charge happens once. Repeated 'non-recurring' items are ordinary operating costs management would rather you excluded from the picture.

cards.headline: The truth hides in the footnotes.
cards.body: Headlines get the polish; the footnotes get the facts. Accounting methods, stock-based compensation, lawsuits, pension gaps and debt covenants often live only there. A company burying bad news does it in small print — which is exactly why you read it.

cards.summary: Red flags are contradictions between the story and the cash.
bullets: Profit rising while cash falls is the loudest warning.
Receivables or inventory outpacing sales needs explaining.
Recurring 'one-time' charges and footnotes hide the truth.

cards.insight: Failures leave fingerprints in the statements long before the headlines. Your job is to read them early.
